Other ways to insulate a wall include adding rigid insulation board to the exterior or interior, or removing interior finishes and adding batt insulation, among others (Baechler, et al. 2021) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2019). Attic, crawlspace, basement, or other building insulation techniques are not covered in this measure. Attic floor insulation for unfinished basements is addressed in a separate measure documentation.3 There are safety concerns that must be addressed when performing drill-and-fill insulation. The structural integrity of the exterior wall and cladding is important, as is any existing water damage (Pfeiffer 2021). Asbestos is a health and safety concern for insulation installers and is more common in homes built between 1930 and 1970 (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2011). Mold or rotted wood may be found in stud cavities, which could also complicate retrofits (Brozyna and Badger 2013). This is not a complete list of safety concerns that should be addressed before upgrading a building’s insulation. 1.2 Drill-and-Fill Considerations The thermal resistance of drill-and-fill insulation is measured by its R-value, which represents the material’s ability to reduce heat flow (U.S. Department of Energy 2010). A higher R-value results in less heat transfer. As a retrofit, drill-and-fill wall insulation can achieve up to R-13 cavity insulation in 2x4 exterior stud cavities (3.5 inches at R-3.7 per inch), which is the maximum insulation level modeled in this measure (Holladay 2013). Wall cavities that are insulated to levels less than R-13 (e.g., R-11, R-7) did not receive the drill- and-fill upgrade in this ResStock measure. An experienced drill-and-fill practitioner noted that installing additional drill-and-fill insulation into an already insulated wall could cause the insulation batt to bunch, create uneven insulation levels, and lead to other issues. This is supported by literature on retrofit projects that choose not to perform drill-and-fill insulation on walls with existing insulation below R-13 (Frontier Energy, Inc., Misti Bruceri & Associates, LLC 2022) (Antonopoulos, et al. 2022). However, there is some evidence that drill-and-fill can be applied to walls with existing insulation, but this is not included in this measure (Holladay 2013). 2 https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/resources/explanations/Wood_Stud_Depth.html 3 https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/96739.pdf 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Manufactured housing or mobile homes receive drill-and-fill insulation in this measure only if the walls are uninsulated and wood stud. In practice, this can be extremely difficult and requires caution (Carlson and Bemis 1979) (Judkoff, Hancock and Franconi 1990). As with all ResStock results, this upgrade measure represents theoretical technical potential, and dataset users should independently assess whether this measure is appropriate for their building segment of interest. Studies often pair air sealing and drill-and-fill insulation and report combined energy savings. One study modeled energy savings from drill-and-fill insulation across different climate zones and found whole-home site energy savings ranging from 8.8% to 13.5% (Polly, et al. 2011).
